newsitem.title: USA: NYC wants proposed Authority to sell bonds in 1998.
newsitem.headline: NYC wants proposed Authority to sell bonds in 1998.

text.p: New York City wants the new financing arm that Albany lawmakers agreed to but still have to approve in legislation to sell a total of $1.25 billion of bonds in fiscal 1998, a city official said on Wednesday.
That is the same amount as the volume of general obligation bonds that the city expects to sell in its next fiscal year, which starts July 1.

The city still plans to sell around $300 million of general obligation bonds in May, the last such sale expected in the 1997 fiscal year, said the city official, who declined to be named. Traders had speculated that the new Authority's bonds might hit the market during the present fiscal year.

Underwriters for the new Authority are expected to be chosen fairly quickly. "I expect that will happen in the next couple of months, maybe sooner," the city official said. A city source, who declined to be named, said it had not yet been decided whether the underwriters for the city's general obligations would also be eligibile to sell the new Authority's bonds.

Though the Giuliani Administration, which proposed the new Transitional Finance Authority as a way to circumvent a state-imposed debt cap, had wanted to sell up to $11 billion of bonds, only $7.5 billion were approved, a sum expected to help fund the city's capital needs for about four years.

The Authority's ability to issue debt will last only until the state constitution is modified to provide for a less restrictive way of calculating its debt limit, which now is based on a five-year average of property values, which has yet to fully reflect the market's rebound from the sharp, local recession in the early 1990s. The earliest possible date for a vote on a constitutional amendment is November 1999, according to the City Council.
New York City is expected to hit its approximately $31 billion debt limit during the spring or summer, which could force it to halt part of its capital program.
Most limitations on the types of projects that the bonds can be sold for were dropped, leaving the money available for projects that are appropriated in the city's capital budget.

However, New York Times, in its Wednesday edition, said that Giuliani made a verbal promise not to use the Authority to finance a new stadium for the Yankees baseball team on Manhattan's West Side. George Steinbrenner, the team's main owner, is exploring building a new site there, as well as other options, including moving the team to another state or renovating the Yankees' historic stadium in the Bronx.

Whether any of the new Authority's bonds would be taxable, and thus could be sold overseas, has yet to be decided, though the city official said that the new entity might not enjoy the same high name recognition abroard as the city itself does.
